student_answer: Object-oriented programming is one of the most widely taught paradigms in computer science. Encapsulation is the principle of bundling an object's data and behavior together while restricting direct access to its internal state.
reference_answer: Encapsulation is the OOP principle of bundling data and the methods that operate on that data within a single unit, typically a class, while restricting direct access to some of the object's components. Access modifiers such as private, protected, and public control the visibility of fields and methods, enforcing information hiding. By making fields private and exposing controlled access through getters and setters, a class can validate changes to its internal state and hide implementation details from the outside world. This reduces coupling between classes and makes code easier to maintain and refactor.

This is because hiding the internal fields prevents other parts of the program from making the object enter an invalid state. For instance, a class can expose getter and setter methods instead of allowing direct access to a private field. In conclusion, encapsulation and access modifiers work together to achieve data hiding and reduce coupling between classes.

student_answer: Databases are used in almost every modern software application. Normalization is the process of organizing relational database tables to reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity.
reference_answer: Normalization is the process of organizing relational database tables to reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity. First normal form (1NF) requires atomic column values, second normal form (2NF) removes partial dependencies on a composite key, and third normal form (3NF) removes transitive functional dependencies so non-key attributes depend only on the primary key. Applying these forms step by step prevents update, insert, and delete anomalies.

For example, first normal form (1NF) requires that each column hold only atomic, indivisible values. This is because storing multiple values in a single column makes querying and updating the data unreliable. In conclusion, applying 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF step by step reduces redundancy and keeps the database consistent.

student_answer: ACID properties describe the guarantees that a database transaction provides to keep data reliable. For example, atomicity ensures that a transaction either completes fully or has no effect at all, such as a bank transfer that debits one account and credits another. This is because if only half the operations succeeded, the database would be left in an inconsistent state. In conclusion, atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability together make transactions safe even in the presence of failures or concurrency.
reference_answer: ACID properties describe the guarantees that a database transaction provides to keep data reliable: atomicity ensures a transaction fully completes or has no effect, consistency ensures the database moves between valid states, isolation ensures concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other, and durability ensures committed changes survive system failures. Together these properties make transactions safe under concurrency and failure.

student_answer: The OSI model was created as a conceptual framework by the ISO.
reference_answer: The OSI model divides network communication into seven layers, each responsible for a specific function, from the physical layer that transmits raw bits, through the network layer that routes packets using IP addresses, up to the application layer that provides services directly to end user software. The transport layer, using protocols like TCP, provides reliable delivery and flow control between endpoints. This layered design allows each layer to evolve independently.

student_answer: TCP and UDP are both transport-layer protocols, but they make very different trade-offs between reliability and speed. For example, TCP is connection-oriented and establishes a handshake before transferring data, guaranteeing reliable, in-order delivery. This is because TCP retransmits lost packets and acknowledges received ones, which adds reliability at the cost of overhead.
reference_answer: TCP and UDP are both transport-layer protocols, but they make very different trade-offs between reliability and speed. TCP is connection-oriented, establishing a handshake and guaranteeing reliable, in-order delivery through acknowledgements and retransmission. UDP is connectionless and sends packets without delivery guarantees, resulting in lower latency that suits real-time applications such as video streaming and gaming.

student_answer: The waterfall model and agile methodology represent two very different approaches to organizing the software development lifecycle. For example, the waterfall model moves sequentially through fixed phases such as requirements, design, implementation, and testing, only moving forward once each phase is complete. This is because waterfall assumes requirements are well understood upfront and rarely change during development. For instance, agile methodology breaks work into short iterations called sprints, delivering working software incrementally and gathering feedback along the way. In conclusion, waterfall offers predictability for well-defined projects, while agile offers flexibility for projects with evolving requirements.

student_answer: Time complexity is usually taught alongside space complexity in algorithms courses.
reference_answer: Big-O notation describes how the running time of an algorithm grows as the size of its input increases, typically focusing on worst-case analysis. A linear search runs in O(n) time because it may inspect every element, binary search on sorted data runs in O(log n) time, and a naive nested-loop comparison runs in O(n^2) time. Big-O allows algorithms to be compared independent of hardware or implementation details.

student_answer: Big-O notation describes how the running time of an algorithm grows as the size of its input increases. For example, a linear search that checks every element once has O(n) time complexity, where n is the number of elements. This is because in the worst case, the algorithm may need to inspect every single element before finding the target or concluding it's absent. For instance, binary search on a sorted array runs in O(log n) time, whereas a naive nested-loop comparison runs in O(n^2) time. This matters because as input size grows, an O(n^2) algorithm becomes dramatically slower than an O(log n) or O(n) algorithm. In conclusion, Big-O notation, focused on worst-case analysis, helps compare algorithms independent of hardware or implementation details.

reference_answer: Quicksort and merge sort are both efficient divide-and-conquer sorting algorithms. Quicksort selects a pivot and partitions elements around it, achieving O(n log n) average-case time but O(n^2) worst-case time on adversarial input. Merge sort always splits the array in half and merges sorted halves, giving guaranteed O(n log n) performance and stability, meaning equal elements retain their relative order.

student_answer: Quicksort and merge sort are both efficient divide-and-conquer sorting algorithms, but they differ in how they partition data and in their stability. For example, quicksort selects a pivot element and partitions the array so that smaller elements go left and larger elements go right, then recursively sorts each side. This is because a good pivot choice keeps the partitions balanced, giving quicksort an average-case time complexity of O(n log n). For instance, merge sort splits the array in half, recursively sorts each half, and merges the results, which makes it a stable sort. This matters because stability preserves the relative order of equal elements, which quicksort does not guarantee. In conclusion, merge sort offers predictable performance and stability, while quicksort is often faster in practice due to lower constant factors.

reference_answer: A stack and a queue are both linear data structures, but they differ in the order in which elements are added and removed. A stack follows last-in-first-out (LIFO) order using push and pop operations, making it useful for function call tracking and undo operations. A queue follows first-in-first-out (FIFO) order using enqueue and dequeue operations, making it useful for task scheduling and breadth-first search.

sentence_roles.text: A stack and a queue are both linear data structures, but they differ in the order in which elements are added and removed.
For example, a stack follows a last-in-first-out (LIFO) order, where the push operation adds an element to the top and pop removes the most recently added element.
This is because LIFO behavior makes stacks useful for tasks like function call tracking and undo operations.
In conclusion, choosing between a stack and a queue depends on whether the problem requires LIFO or FIFO ordering of elements.
